items.title: Octopuses change colour while being colour-blind
items.claim: Cephalopods produce sophisticated colour displays — mimicking corals, fish, sand — using chromatophore cells embedded in the skin. Their actual eyes have only one photoreceptor type. They cannot distinguish red from green.
items.prompt: How do octopuses match colour without seeing it?

options.text: They have hidden colour vision we haven't found
Their SKIN contains opsin proteins — the same light-sensitive receptors used in eyes — likely giving the surface itself wavelength-sensitivity that the eyes lack
Other octopuses signal the colour to them

items.reveal_title: Distributed colour vision via opsin-expressing skin
items.reveal:
Cephalopod skin expresses several genes (including r-opsin and rhodopsin-like proteins) usually found in eyes. Ramirez and Oakley (2015) showed Octopus bimaculoides skin responds to specific wavelengths.

The hypothesis: the chromatic information bypasses the brain entirely. The skin senses ambient colour and adjusts the chromatophore display locally without needing centralised colour vision.

It's also possible they exploit the chromatic aberration of their unusual U-shaped pupils to extract colour information from a single photoreceptor type — Stubbs and Stubbs (2016) — but the experimental support is mixed. Either way, cephalopod colour matching is a fascinating biological riddle.
items.why: Vision is assumed to happen in eyes and brains. In cephalopods it may happen distributed across the body.

items.title: Your lungs have the surface area of half a tennis court
items.claim: Two lungs, about 4 to 6 litres total volume — but the internal surface area where gas exchange happens is 50 to 75 square metres. Achieved by 300 to 500 million alveoli, each a tiny sphere with a thin shared wall to a capillary.
items.prompt: Why is so much surface area needed?

options.text: Diffusion of gases across a membrane scales with surface area and inversely with thickness; meeting the body's O2 demand (~250 ml/min at rest, ~3 L/min at exercise) requires both a huge area and an ultra-thin barrier (~0.5 micrometres)
Extra alveoli are spare in case some collapse

items.reveal:
Rate of diffusion = (surface area * concentration gradient) / (membrane thickness). To maximise O2 uptake, organisms maximise area, maximise gradient (high O2 in air vs low in blood) and minimise thickness.

Alveoli: 0.2-0.5 mm diameter spheres, lined with type I cells (extremely thin), surrounded by capillaries. The blood-air barrier is only 2-3 cells thick — sometimes <0.5 micrometres.

If you flattened all alveoli out, they would cover ~70 square metres — close to a singles tennis court.

Diseases that destroy alveoli (emphysema) reduce gas exchange capacity. Pulmonary fibrosis thickens the barrier. Both cause shortness of breath at exertion.

Total lung capillary blood volume is only ~75 ml at rest, but blood transits in ~0.75 seconds — enough for full equilibration in healthy lungs. At maximal exercise, transit time can drop to 0.25 seconds; in well-trained athletes at altitude, diffusion can become rate-limiting.
items.why: Big surface in small volume seems like a packaging miracle. Evolution solved it with tessellated bubbles — and made breathing possible at human body size.

items.title: The most abundant enzyme on Earth is bad at its job
items.claim: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide into sugar in every photosynthesising organism. It's the most abundant protein on the planet (about half a kilogram in every square metre of leaf). It's also slow (3 reactions per second per active site) and confuses CO2 with O2.
items.prompt: Why do plants invest so heavily in such a flawed enzyme?

options.text: There's no alternative — Rubisco is the only carbon-fixation enzyme that works

Rubisco evolved when the atmosphere had little O2; the confusion between CO2 and O2 was rare then. Now plants mass-produce it (often 50 percent of leaf protein) to compensate for its slowness, and C4 plants concentrate CO2 around it to outcompete O2 binding
Rubisco is highly efficient — the textbook is wrong

items.reveal:
Rubisco's active site binds CO2 by inserting it into a bound substrate (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate). About 25 percent of the time at room temperature, it grabs O2 instead — initiating photorespiration, a wasteful cycle that costs energy and releases CO2.

This was tolerable in the Proterozoic atmosphere (low O2, high CO2). As oxygen rose and CO2 dropped, the problem grew.

C4 plants (corn, sugarcane) evolved an extra carbon-fixation step in mesophyll cells (using PEP carboxylase, which doesn't confuse O2). This shuttles CO2 into specialised bundle-sheath cells at high concentration, where Rubisco then operates without interference.

CAM plants (cacti, pineapples) do the same trick temporally — fixing CO2 at night when stomata can be open without losing water.
items.why: Evolution doesn't engineer optimal enzymes — it tinkers around constraints inherited from earlier conditions. Rubisco is a beautiful example of a molecular legacy system.
